title: Abraham Lincoln
summary: The 16th president of the United States (1861–1865), an Illinois lawyer and Republican who led the Union through the Civil War, issued the Emancipation Proclamation, backed the Thirteenth Amendment, and was assassinated in April 1865.

review.question: Why did Lincoln win the presidency in 1860 with less than 40 percent of the popular vote?
review.answer: Four major candidates split the vote; Lincoln carried every free state, which gave him 180 of 303 electoral votes, a clear Electoral College majority, even though he was not on the ballot in much of the South.

review.question: How did the actions of enslaved people shape Lincoln's emancipation policy, according to historians such as Ira Berlin?
review.answer: By fleeing to Union lines and offering labor and military service, enslaved people forced Union officers, Congress and the president to decide their status; Lincoln, who had first favored gradual, compensated emancipation and colonization, moved toward the Emancipation Proclamation as that pressure grew.

review.question: Why do historians debate Lincoln's title of "Great Emancipator"?
review.answer: Some see his leadership as the decisive force that ended slavery, while others argue he was a reluctant emancipator and that enslaved people were the prime movers; the debate is about how to weigh presidential leadership against the agency of the enslaved.

timeline.event: Born near Hodgenville, Kentucky.
First elected to the Illinois legislature.
As a first-term Whig congressman, introduces the Spot Resolutions challenging the case for war with Mexico.
Gives the "House Divided" speech; later loses the Senate race to Stephen A. Douglas.
Elected 16th president with a majority of electoral votes from the free states.
Inaugurated after seven Southern states had seceded.
Thirty-eight Dakota men are hanged at Mankato after Lincoln commutes most of the death sentences.
The Emancipation Proclamation takes effect in areas in rebellion.
Delivers the Gettysburg Address.
Reelected president.
Shot by John Wilkes Booth at Ford's Theatre; dies the next morning.

misconception.myth: Lincoln dashed off the Gettysburg Address on the back of an envelope on the train to Gettysburg.
misconception.fact: Lincoln worked on the speech in the weeks before November 19, 1863; a Library of Congress copy begins in ink on Executive Mansion stationery written in Washington, and the drafts are in steady handwriting unlike a moving train's.
misconception.why: The envelope story turns a carefully revised speech into a lucky improvisation and hides how deliberately Lincoln shaped his public words.

title: American Civil War
summary: The war of 1861–1865 between the United States and eleven slaveholding Southern states that seceded to form the Confederacy; it preserved the Union and destroyed slavery at a cost of roughly 750,000 lives.

review.question: Why did Deep South states secede after the 1860 election, before Lincoln had taken office?
review.answer: They saw the victory of a party opposed to slavery's expansion as a threat to slavery itself. Mississippi's declaration said its position was thoroughly identified with slavery, and South Carolina's centered on Northern refusal to return fugitives from slavery.

review.question: How did enslaved people help turn a war for the Union into a war against slavery?
review.answer: By fleeing to Union lines from 1861 on, they forced the army and Congress to decide their status, which led to contraband policy, the Confiscation Acts, abolition in Washington, D.C., the Emancipation Proclamation, and the enlistment of about 179,000 Black soldiers.

review.question: Why do historians now cite about 750,000 deaths instead of the long-used 620,000?
review.answer: J. David Hacker compared census survival rates for 1860–1870 with the decades before and after, and the shortfall pointed to about 750,000 deaths (range 650,000–850,000), since earlier counts relied on incomplete military records.

timeline.event: A South Carolina convention votes 169 to 0 to secede after Abraham Lincoln's election.
Delegates from seven seceded states meet in Montgomery, Alabama, and choose Jefferson Davis as Confederate president.
Confederate forces fire on Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor; it surrenders the next day and Lincoln calls for 75,000 volunteers.
At Fort Monroe, General Benjamin Butler begins receiving people fleeing slavery as "contraband of war."
Congress abolishes slavery in the District of Columbia.
The Battle of Antietam, the bloodiest single day in American history, gives Lincoln the victory he awaited to announce emancipation.
The Emancipation Proclamation takes effect in areas under Confederate control.
The War Department creates the Bureau of Colored Troops to organize Black regiments.
Pickett's Charge fails, ending the three-day Battle of Gettysburg.
Vicksburg surrenders to Ulysses S. Grant, splitting the Confederacy in two.
Congress grants Black soldiers pay equal to white soldiers, retroactively.
William T. Sherman's army captures Atlanta before marching to the sea.
Robert E. Lee surrenders the Army of Northern Virginia to Grant at Appomattox.

misconception.myth: The Civil War was fought over states' rights or tariffs, not slavery.
misconception.fact: The seceding states said otherwise at the time. Mississippi declared its position "thoroughly identified with the institution of slavery," South Carolina complained that Northern states would not enforce the Fugitive Slave Act, and Confederate Vice President Alexander Stephens rested the new government on Black inequality. The only state right at stake was the right to protect slavery.
misconception.why: The postwar "Lost Cause" story recast secession as a defense of constitutional principle. Believing it hides what the war was about and why emancipation and the Reconstruction amendments followed from it.

title: Brown v. Board of Education
aliases: Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka
summary: The unanimous 1954 U.S. Supreme Court decision holding that state laws segregating public schools by race violate the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, rejecting the "separate but equal" doctrine in public education.

review.question: Why did the NAACP's lawyers value the Kansas case even though Topeka's Black and white schools were roughly comparable in buildings and resources?
review.answer: Because the facilities were substantially comparable, the Kansas case forced the Court to decide whether segregation itself was unconstitutional rather than merely ordering states to equalize unequal schools, and it showed that school segregation was a national issue and not only a Southern one.

review.question: Why was the District of Columbia case, Bolling v. Sharpe, decided separately from the four state cases?
review.answer: The Fourteenth Amendment's Equal Protection Clause restrains the states, not the federal government, so segregation in the federal capital had to be challenged under the Fifth Amendment instead.

review.question: How did the Court's approach to remedies allow segregation to continue for years after 1954?
review.answer: The 1954 ruling did not say how or when schools must desegregate; Brown II in 1955 left it to federal district courts to proceed "with all deliberate speed," and opponents used that vague standard to delay, admit only token numbers of Black students, pass new segregation laws, or, as in Prince Edward County, close public schools from 1959 to 1964.

timeline.event: Students led by 16-year-old Barbara Rose Johns walk out of the overcrowded Robert Russa Moton High School in Farmville, Virginia.
NAACP lawyers file Davis v. County School Board of Prince Edward County, later joined to Brown.
The Supreme Court hears the first arguments in the consolidated school cases.
Reargument begins on questions the Court posed, including the history of the Fourteenth Amendment and possible remedies.
The Court rules unanimously that segregated public schools violate the Equal Protection Clause; Bolling v. Sharpe is decided the same day.
In Brown II the Court orders desegregation to proceed with all deliberate speed under federal district courts.
The Southern Manifesto denouncing the decision is introduced in Congress.
Prince Edward County, Virginia, cuts off public school funding rather than desegregate.
Prince Edward County's public schools reopen after the Supreme Court's Griffin decision.
Attorneys ask the federal court to reopen the Topeka case to test whether segregation's effects remained (Brown III).

misconception.myth: The case began when Oliver Brown alone sued after his daughter Linda was turned away from a nearby white school and forced to walk far to a Black school.
misconception.fact: The Topeka NAACP deliberately organized a class action with 13 parents on behalf of 20 children; Oliver Brown was recruited to join and named because he was the only man in the group, and the Supreme Court decided Kansas's case together with cases from South Carolina, Virginia, Delaware and the District of Columbia involving nearly 200 people.
misconception.why: Reducing Brown to one family's story hides the years of organized legal strategy and the many students, parents, teachers and lawyers, in the South and beyond it, who took risks to bring the cases.

title: Constitutional Convention
summary: The meeting of delegates from twelve states in Philadelphia from May 25 to September 17, 1787, that was called to revise the Articles of Confederation and instead drafted the United States Constitution.

review.question: Why did the convention end up writing a whole new constitution when Congress had asked only for revisions?
review.answer: Many delegates believed the Articles left the central government too weak; Randolph's Virginia Plan on May 29 proposed a new national legislature, executive and judiciary, and by mid-June the delegates had accepted that they were drafting a new frame of government rather than amending the old one.

review.question: How did the Great Compromise settle the quarrel between large and small states?
review.answer: It gave the House of Representatives seats in proportion to each state's population and gave every state equal representation in the Senate; it passed on July 16, 1787, by a single state's margin.

review.question: How did the convention's decisions strengthen slaveholding states?
review.answer: Counting three-fifths of enslaved people added to slave states' seats in the House and, through the electoral college, their weight in presidential elections; the convention also barred Congress from ending the Atlantic slave trade before 1808 and added a fugitive slave clause.

review.question: Why do historians disagree about whether the Constitution was a proslavery document?
review.answer: Paul Finkelman argues its many protections for slavery made it a proslavery bargain, while Sean Wilentz argues that by refusing to recognise property in people the framers left an opening later antislavery politicians used; critics of Wilentz note that his key Madison quotation may have been added to Madison's notes later.

timeline.event: The Confederation Congress calls a convention to meet in Philadelphia in May to revise the Articles of Confederation.
The convention's scheduled opening day; too few delegations are present, so members adjourn from day to day.
Seven states form a quorum and the delegates unanimously elect George Washington president of the convention.
Edmund Randolph presents the Virginia Plan, and the convention adopts a rule keeping its proceedings secret.
James Wilson and Charles Pinckney propose counting three-fifths of enslaved people for representation.
The convention adopts the three-fifths rule, six states to two with two divided.
The Great (Connecticut) Compromise passes by a margin of one state.
A bargain between New England and Deep South delegates protects the Atlantic slave trade until 1808.
Thirty-eight delegates sign thirty-nine names to the finished Constitution; three present delegates refuse.
Congress unanimously resolves to send the Constitution to the states for ratifying conventions.
Delaware becomes the first state to ratify.
New Hampshire becomes the ninth state to ratify, enough for the Constitution to take effect.

misconception.myth: The delegates were sent to Philadelphia to write a new constitution.
misconception.fact: Congress called the meeting only to revise the Articles of Confederation and report proposed alterations to Congress and the states; the delegates decided on their own, by mid-June 1787, to draft an entirely new frame of government, and their Constitution took effect once nine state conventions had ratified it.
misconception.why: Because the convention's product replaced the Articles completely and is commemorated on September 17, it is easy to assume a new constitution was the assignment from the start, which hides how bold, and how contested, the delegates' decision was.

title: Declaration of Independence
aliases: The unanimous Declaration of the thirteen united States of America
summary: The statement adopted by the Second Continental Congress on July 4, 1776, announcing that the thirteen American colonies were free and independent states, setting out a philosophy of natural rights and government by consent, and listing grievances against King George III.

review.question: Why did Congress cut Jefferson's passage blaming the king for the slave trade?
review.answer: Jefferson recorded that it was struck to accommodate South Carolina and Georgia, which wanted the slave trade to continue, and that some Northern delegates were uneasy because Northern merchants had carried enslaved people; the deletion kept those delegations behind independence.

review.question: How did declaring independence help the American war effort abroad?
review.answer: France would consider a formal alliance only once the colonies declared independence, so the Declaration opened the way to recognition and to the 1778 Treaty of Alliance with France, followed by Dutch recognition in 1782 and British acknowledgement in the 1783 Treaty of Paris.

review.question: Why is July 4 not the day the Declaration was signed?
review.answer: July 4 was the day Congress approved the text; the signing copy was only ordered on July 19, and most delegates signed it on August 2, 1776, with others signing later.

review.question: How did later reformers use the Declaration's language?
review.answer: The women who met at Seneca Falls in 1848 modelled their Declaration of Sentiments on it, declaring that all men and women are created equal, and Frederick Douglass in 1852 measured the nation's celebration of independence against the slavery it still allowed.

timeline.event: Richard Henry Lee of Virginia moves in Congress that the colonies are, and ought to be, free and independent states.
The drafting committee presents Jefferson's draft, edited by Adams and Franklin, to Congress.
A first vote on Lee's resolution: nine colonies in favour, Pennsylvania and South Carolina opposed, Delaware deadlocked and New York abstaining.
Twelve colonies vote for independence, with New York abstaining.
Congress approves the revised text and orders it printed; John Dunlap prints about 200 broadsides.
John Nixon gives the first public reading in the State House Yard in Philadelphia.
Congress orders the text engrossed on parchment under a new title for members to sign.
John Hancock and most of the delegates sign the engrossed parchment.
Congress authorizes a printing that carries the signers' names for the first time.

misconception.myth: The delegates signed the Declaration of Independence on July 4, 1776.
misconception.fact: Congress approved the text on July 4, but it ordered a parchment copy for signing only on July 19; most delegates signed on August 2, 1776, a few signed later that year, and Thomas McKean signed sometime after January 1777.
misconception.why: Later recollections by Jefferson and Adams placed the signing on July 4, and the copies printed that week carried only the names of John Hancock and Charles Thomson, so the date of approval and the act of signing blurred together in popular memory.

title: Fourteenth Amendment
aliases: Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution
summary: The 1868 amendment to the U.S. Constitution that made all persons born or naturalized in the United States citizens and barred states from denying any person due process of law or the equal protection of the laws; it also reshaped representation, barred certain former officials who joined the rebellion from office, and settled Civil War debts.

review.question: What problems was the amendment meant to solve after the Thirteenth Amendment ended slavery?
review.answer: Southern states were passing Black Codes to limit freed people's rights while white southerners terrorized them, and Dred Scott's rule still denied Black Americans citizenship; the amendment made all persons born or naturalized in the country citizens, barred states from denying due process or equal protection, and gave Congress power to enforce those guarantees.

review.question: How did the Slaughter-House Cases change what the amendment meant in practice?
review.answer: The Court held that the Privileges or Immunities Clause protected only rights of national citizenship, leaving most rights to the states and turning the clause into a practical nullity, so later protection of Bill of Rights guarantees against the states came instead through the Due Process Clause, case by case.

review.question: Why were former Confederate states required to ratify the amendment?
review.answer: White southerners rejected it almost unanimously in 1866 and 1867; after Northern voters backed Republicans in the 1866 elections, Congress made ratification a condition for restoring a state's representation, and Southern ratifications in 1868 completed the three-fourths.

review.question: Who was left out of the citizenship clause at first, and how did that change?
review.answer: Native people under tribal rather than U.S. authority were excluded, and Elk v. Wilkins (1884) held that Native Americans were not U.S. citizens even after leaving their nations; Congress made all Native Americans citizens only with the Indian Citizenship Act of 1924.

timeline.event: Congress creates the Joint Committee of Fifteen on Reconstruction.
Congress passes the Civil Rights Act of 1866.
The Senate passes the amendment, 33 to 11.
The House passes the amendment, 120 to 32.
The joint resolution is submitted to the states.
The Reconstruction Act places former Confederate states except Tennessee under military districts.
Louisiana and South Carolina ratify, completing the three-fourths needed.
Secretary of State William H. Seward certifies ratification by 28 states.
The Slaughter-House Cases narrow the Privileges or Immunities Clause.
Minor v. Happersett holds that citizenship does not carry a right to vote.
Elk v. Wilkins holds that Native Americans who had left their nations were still not U.S. citizens.
United States v. Wong Kim Ark applies birthright citizenship to a U.S.-born son of Chinese parents.
The Indian Citizenship Act makes Native Americans U.S. citizens.

misconception.myth: By making women citizens, the Fourteenth Amendment gave them the right to vote.
misconception.fact: Section 2 penalized states only for denying the vote to male citizens, and in Minor v. Happersett (1875) the Supreme Court held that citizenship did not carry the right to vote; women won a constitutional guarantee only with the Nineteenth Amendment in 1920.
misconception.why: Assuming citizenship and voting rights always went together hides how long women, and Native Americans after the 1924 citizenship act, were citizens who could still be kept from the polls.

title: Plessy v. Ferguson
summary: The 1896 U.S. Supreme Court decision that upheld a Louisiana law requiring separate railroad cars for Black and white passengers, giving constitutional approval to state-imposed racial segregation under what became known as the "separate but equal" doctrine.

review.question: Why did Homer Plessy board a whites-only car on a train that stayed inside Louisiana rather than an interstate train?
review.answer: Weeks earlier, in Abbott v. Hicks, the Louisiana Supreme Court had ruled that the Separate Car Act did not apply to interstate passengers, so the Comité des Citoyens needed an intrastate trip to test the law's constitutionality directly.

review.question: How did Justice Brown's majority answer the argument that forced separation stamped Black citizens as inferior?
review.answer: He said any such stigma did not come from the law itself but from how Black Americans chose to interpret it, and he treated segregation as a reasonable use of a state's police power that could take established customs into account.

review.question: Why is Plessy considered so consequential even though it concerned railroad cars?
review.answer: By holding that state-mandated separation did not violate the Fourteenth Amendment if accommodations were nominally equal, it gave legal cover to segregation in schools, transportation and public life for more than half a century, until Brown v. Board of Education rejected the doctrine in public education in 1954.

timeline.event: Louisiana's legislature passes the Separate Car Act (Act No. 111), requiring separate railroad cars for Black and white passengers.
Eighteen New Orleans residents form the Comité des Citoyens to challenge the law in court.
Daniel Desdunes boards a whites-only car on an interstate train in a first test case.
In Abbott v. Hicks the Louisiana Supreme Court rules that the act does not apply to interstate passengers.
Homer Plessy is arrested after sitting in the whites-only coach of an East Louisiana Railroad train to Covington.
Judge John Howard Ferguson of the Orleans Parish Criminal Court rules against Plessy.
The Louisiana Supreme Court upholds Ferguson's ruling.
The U.S. Supreme Court affirms, 7 to 1, with Justice Henry Billings Brown writing and Justice John Marshall Harlan dissenting.
Plessy pleads guilty in New Orleans and pays a $25 fine.
Brown v. Board of Education rejects separate but equal in public education.
Louisiana Governor John Bel Edwards grants Plessy a posthumous pardon.

misconception.myth: The Supreme Court's majority opinion in Plessy announced the phrase "separate but equal."
misconception.fact: The majority opinion speaks of the statute's "equal but separate" accommodations; the words "separate but equal" appear in Justice Harlan's dissent, and the label for the doctrine became common afterward.
misconception.why: Knowing the exact wording shows that the Court was approving a state statute's own formula, and that the promise of equality was a legislative claim the majority accepted rather than tested.

title: September 11 attacks
summary: The coordinated al Qaeda terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001, in which 19 hijackers seized four U.S. airliners and crashed them into the World Trade Center in New York City, the Pentagon in Virginia and a field in Somerset County, Pennsylvania, killing nearly 3,000 people.

review.question: Why did the 9/11 Commission call imagination the most important failure before the attacks?
review.answer: Officials had warnings about al Qaeda and earlier attacks such as the 1998 embassy bombings and the 2000 USS Cole attack, but no one treated the use of hijacked airliners as weapons as a real threat; the Commission found that U.S. measures between 1998 and 2001 never disturbed or delayed the plot.

review.question: How did the actions of the people aboard United 93 change the outcome of the attacks?
review.answer: After learning by phone of the other hijackings, the passengers and crew voted to fight back and forced the plane down in a Pennsylvania field about 20 minutes' flying time from Washington, so it never reached its probable target, the U.S. Capitol or the White House.

review.question: How did the attacks reshape the federal government at home?
review.answer: Within weeks the president created a White House Office of Homeland Security, Congress passed the USA PATRIOT Act and created the TSA in 2001, and the Homeland Security Act of 2002 merged 22 agencies into a new Cabinet department; the 9/11 Commission's 2004 report then led to proposals such as a National Counterterrorism Center and a national intelligence director.

timeline.event: Al Qaeda leader Usama Bin Ladin approves the airliner plot conceived by Khalid Sheikh Mohammed (late 1998 or early 1999).
By early July all 19 hijackers, who had begun entering the country in January 2000, are inside the United States.

Hijacked airliners strike the World Trade Center's North Tower (8:46 a.m.) and South Tower (9:03 a.m.) and the Pentagon (9:37 a.m.); United 93 crashes in Pennsylvania at 10:03 a.m. after a passenger and crew revolt.
President George W. Bush signs the Authorization for Use of Military Force against those responsible.
Bush signs the USA PATRIOT Act, expanding surveillance and security powers.
U.S. air strikes against Taliban and al Qaeda targets in Afghanistan begin Operation Enduring Freedom.
The recovery effort at Ground Zero formally ends with the removal of the Last Column.
The Department of Homeland Security opens, combining parts or all of 22 federal agencies.
The bipartisan 9/11 Commission issues its final report and closes on August 21, 2004.
NIST issues its final report on the collapse of the Twin Towers.
The National September 11 Memorial opens to the public, a day after its dedication on the tenth anniversary.

misconception.myth: The Twin Towers were brought down by a planned controlled demolition using explosives or thermite rather than by the hijacked planes.
misconception.fact: The federal engineering investigation by NIST found that the impacts severed columns and stripped fireproofing, and that multi-floor fires weakened floors that pulled the perimeter columns inward until they failed; it found no corroborating evidence for explosives, and seismic signals came from falling debris after each collapse began.
misconception.why: The towers' sudden, total collapse was unprecedented and hard to grasp, and demolition stories replace a documented chain of failures and warnings with a hidden plot that the engineering and investigative record does not support.

title: Slavery in the United States
aliases: Chattel slavery in the United States
summary: The system of hereditary, race-based chattel slavery that held people of African descent, and in the colonial era many Native Americans, as property in the English colonies and the United States from the early 1600s until the Thirteenth Amendment abolished it in 1865.

review.question: Why did Virginia's 1662 law matter so much for slavery's growth?
review.answer: It made a child's status follow the mother's rather than the father's, so every child of an enslaved woman was born enslaved; slavery became hereditary and could grow through births rather than only through imports.

review.question: How did the enslaved population grow from about 700,000 in 1790 to nearly 4 million in 1860 even though importing enslaved people was banned from 1808?
review.answer: Because children of enslaved mothers were born enslaved, the population grew through births, and the domestic slave trade then moved about a million people from the Upper South to the cotton-growing Deep South.

review.question: How did slavery reach into the free states before the Civil War?
review.answer: The Constitution's fugitive slave clause required people escaping bondage to be returned, and the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 used federal commissioners without juries to send about 1,000 Black Americans South, provoking resistance in northern communities.

timeline.event: The English privateer White Lion lands about twenty captive Africans at Point Comfort, Virginia, and sells them for food.
Virginia's General Assembly rules that a child is enslaved or free according to the mother's status, making slavery hereditary.
A Virginia law classes enslaved people as real estate.
Pennsylvania passes a gradual emancipation law.
The federal ban on importing enslaved people takes effect.
Slavery ends in New York under its 1817 law.
Nat Turner's rebellion begins in Southampton County, Virginia.
Congress passes a Fugitive Slave Act that denies accused people a jury trial.
The census counts 3,953,760 enslaved people, the peak and the last census to count them.
General Order No. 3 announces freedom in Galveston, Texas, the origin of Juneteenth.
The Thirteenth Amendment is ratified, abolishing slavery nationwide.
New Jersey's governor signs a state constitutional amendment ending slavery there.

misconception.myth: Slavery was a purely Southern institution that the North never practised.
misconception.fact: Slavery was legal in the North too; enslaved people were 30 percent of Kings County (Brooklyn) residents in 1790, New York's final emancipation came only in 1827, and about 16 people in New Jersey were still legally enslaved in December 1865.
misconception.why: Treating slavery as only Southern hides how gradual and incomplete northern emancipation was, and how northern banks and merchants profited from the cotton economy.

title: Thirteenth Amendment
aliases: Thirteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution
summary: The 1865 amendment to the U.S. Constitution that abolished slavery and involuntary servitude throughout the United States, except as punishment for a crime, and gave Congress power to enforce that ban.

review.question: Why did Lincoln and Congress believe a constitutional amendment was needed even after the Emancipation Proclamation?
review.answer: The proclamation rested on Lincoln's war powers and applied only to areas in rebellion, not to loyal border states; its legal force after the war was doubtful, so an amendment was the only secure way to end slavery everywhere.

review.question: How did the 1864 election and the end of the war help the amendment pass and be ratified?
review.answer: After the House first failed to reach two-thirds, Lincoln's reelection campaign put the amendment on the Republican platform and a lame-duck session passed it in January 1865; later, President Andrew Johnson required Southern states seeking readmission to abolish slavery, and Georgia's ratification in December 1865 completed the three-fourths.

review.question: Why is the amendment's exception "as a punishment for crime" significant?
review.answer: Southern states used criminal convictions to lease mostly Black prisoners to private companies, as Georgia did from 1868 to 1908, and scholars still debate whether the framers meant the clause to permit that kind of forced labor.

timeline.event: Congress passes the Corwin Amendment, which would have shielded slavery in the states; it is never ratified.
The Emancipation Proclamation takes effect, but only in areas in rebellion.
The Senate Judiciary Committee under Lyman Trumbull reports the amendment to the full Senate.
The Senate passes the amendment, 38 to 6.
The House passes the amendment, 119 to 56, after earlier votes fell short.
Lincoln approves the joint resolution sending the amendment to the states.
Georgia becomes the 27th state to ratify, completing the three-fourths needed.
Secretary of State William H. Seward proclaims the amendment ratified.

misconception.myth: The Emancipation Proclamation ended slavery throughout the United States.
misconception.fact: The 1863 proclamation applied only to areas in rebellion and left slavery legal in loyal border states; slavery ended nationwide only with the Thirteenth Amendment, which freed people still enslaved in Delaware and Kentucky in December 1865.
misconception.why: Confusing a wartime executive order with a constitutional amendment hides why abolitionists, Congress and Lincoln fought for an amendment, and how close slavery came to surviving the war.

title: Thomas Jefferson
summary: A Virginia planter, lawyer and founder (1743–1826) who drafted the Declaration of Independence, wrote Virginia's statute for religious freedom, served as secretary of state and vice president, and was the third president of the United States (1801–1809), while holding more than 600 people in slavery over his lifetime.

review.question: Why did the House of Representatives, not the voters or the electors, decide the presidential election of 1800?
review.answer: Electors then cast two undifferentiated votes, so Jefferson and his running mate Aaron Burr tied at 73 electoral votes each; the Federalist-controlled House deadlocked for 35 ballots before choosing Jefferson on the 36th, on February 17, 1801.

review.question: How did the Louisiana Purchase test Jefferson's own reading of the Constitution?
review.answer: Jefferson doubted that the Constitution gave the president power to acquire territory and considered an amendment, but public support and the land's value led him to set aside his strict reading, a choice that helped build the principle of implied federal powers.

review.question: How did Jefferson's 1803 letter to William Henry Harrison propose to obtain Native land?
review.answer: He proposed government trading houses that would draw Native leaders into debt, which they would pay off by ceding land, and he expected Native nations either to be absorbed as citizens or to move west of the Mississippi.

timeline.event: Born at Shadwell plantation in western Virginia.
Admitted to the Virginia bar.
Enters the Virginia House of Burgesses, where he serves until 1774.
As a delegate to the Second Continental Congress, drafts the Declaration of Independence.
His wife, Martha Wayles Jefferson, dies after childbirth.
Begins about four years as American minister to France.
Virginia's General Assembly adopts his bill for religious freedom, first drafted in 1777.
Becomes secretary of state under George Washington; resigns in 1793.
Becomes vice president under John Adams after finishing second in the 1796 electoral vote.
The House of Representatives elects him president on its 36th ballot, breaking a 73-73 electoral tie with Aaron Burr.
The United States buys Louisiana from France for $15 million.
In a private letter to William Henry Harrison, lays out a plan to acquire Native lands through trade debts.
Signs the act banning the importation of enslaved people, effective January 1, 1808.
Congress passes his Embargo Act, barring American ships from leaving U.S. ports.
Signs the Non-Intercourse Act replacing the embargo, three days before leaving office.
Dies at Monticello, fifty years after the Declaration's approval.

misconception.myth: Thomas Jefferson wrote that the government is best which governs least.
misconception.fact: The Thomas Jefferson Foundation finds no such line in his writings; the earliest known printing of the wording is John L. O'Sullivan's 1837 introduction to the Democratic Review, and the earliest known attribution to Jefferson dates only from 1853.
misconception.why: The phrase was long associated with the political heirs of Jefferson's Democratic-Republican party, so it drifted onto the party's founder, and a familiar name makes a slogan sound authoritative.
